How to Measure Veterinary Clinic Performance

Reading time7 min
Contact us

A veterinary practice owner who only checks the bank balance at the end of the month is managing the clinic by looking in the rearview mirror. By the time a slow month appears in the bank account, the appointments that could have filled the gap are already lost. Measuring performance in real time, across the right categories, is what helps a practice catch problems early instead of reacting after the damage is done.

Most veterinary practice owners can describe how busy the clinic felt last week, but few can say exactly what that means in numbers until the accountant sends a report weeks later. That delay is expensive. Data from the American Veterinary Medical Association's benchmarking research, presented at the 2025 AVMA Veterinary Business and Economic Forum, shows that U.S. veterinary practices averaged about $1.5 million in gross revenue in 2024, with only modest growth once adjusted for inflation since 2016. This means many practices that feel busier are not actually growing in real terms. Performance measurement helps close the gap between how a clinic feels and how it is actually performing by turning general impressions into numbers that an owner or practice manager can act on before a slow quarter turns into a slow year. Practices that measure performance every week instead of only at the end of the year are much more likely to spot problems while they are still small enough to fix.

The first metric every veterinary practice should track is client volume, and current trends make this especially important. According to the same AVMA benchmarking data, the average number of active clients per practice has been declining since 2019 by about 95 clients each year, reaching 3,351 active clients in 2024. Active clients per full-time equivalent veterinarian also fell by about 15 each year, reaching 1,499. This is not the kind of problem that appears in one bad month. It is a gradual decline that only becomes obvious when a practice consistently tracks active client numbers over several years instead of checking them occasionally. A practice that reviews this metric every quarter can tell the difference between a seasonal slowdown and a long-term decline that needs a different response, such as reactivation campaigns for inactive clients or a stronger focus on generating referrals from existing clients.

New client acquisition should be tracked separately from total active clients because the two metrics answer different questions. The VMG 2025 Economic Survey, which benchmarks independent veterinary practices rather than combining them with corporate-owned clinics, found that new client numbers nationally decreased by more than 8% in 2024. The survey treats this as an important benchmark because it reflects the performance of independent practices without being affected by the industry's ongoing corporate consolidation. A clinic that only watches total revenue can easily miss this trend because loyal clients may spend enough per visit to hide a shrinking pipeline of new clients for months or even years before it eventually affects revenue. Tracking new client numbers every month, and separating them by referral source where possible, gives practice managers time to adjust marketing or community outreach before the pipeline starts to dry up.

Financial efficiency metrics make up the next category, and gross revenue per square foot has become one of the most useful ways to compare practices of different sizes. Frederic Ouedraogo, PhD, presented data at the 2025 AVMA forum showing that gross revenue per square foot averaged $538 in 2024, a figure the AVMA recommends practices use as a benchmark specifically because it can be compared across clinics of any size. Unlike total revenue, this metric does not automatically favor larger facilities. Dr. Ouedraogo also reported that the overall medical staff-to-veterinarian ratio was 2.21 to 1 in 2024. This benchmark helps practice owners judge whether they have the right number of support staff for their clinical workload. A practice operating well below this ratio is likely using veterinarian time for tasks that technicians or assistants could handle instead, reducing the number of appointments a veterinarian can see each day even when the schedule looks full.

Staff turnover is also an important performance metric, not just a human resources issue, because it directly affects how much revenue a veterinary practice can generate. Garth Jordan, CEO of the American Animal Hospital Association, told AVMA News that the average annual turnover rate among veterinary team members stands at 23% and is increasing each year. This directly affects appointment capacity when practices spend weeks trying to replace technicians or receptionists. This also connects to a wellbeing issue documented in a 2024 study published in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association. The study surveyed 2,271 non-veterinarian practice team members and found that 71% scored high or very high on the exhaustion component of a validated burnout assessment tool. A practice that tracks staff turnover alongside client volume and revenue per visit can identify patterns that each metric alone cannot explain. A burned-out and understaffed team often first shows up through slower scheduling and shorter client conversations long before it appears as a financial problem.

Case-level clinical metrics complete a strong performance measurement system, and this is an area where many practices collect far more data than they actually use. Average client transaction, calculated as total revenue divided by client visits, shows whether revenue per visit is increasing or decreasing regardless of the number of appointments. Tracking this metric by individual veterinarian or exam room also helps identify which providers consistently achieve stronger results and which may need additional coaching on treatment recommendations. The Veterinary Hospital Managers Association's July 2024 KPI Quarterly Commentary reported that patient visit volume has been declining across the industry, partly because of inflation and greater price sensitivity among pet owners. This makes average client transaction more important than ever for practices trying to protect revenue while visit numbers decline. A dashboard that updates this metric every week and breaks it down by provider allows managers to have specific, evidence-based coaching conversations instead of general discussions about improving performance.

None of these metrics work well on their own, and this is where many veterinary practices struggle when they build their reporting one spreadsheet at a time. Active client numbers without new client acquisition cannot tell you whether a decline is temporary or long term. Revenue numbers without staff turnover cannot explain why a fully booked schedule still resulted in a disappointing month. Average client transaction without case acceptance cannot show whether one provider's stronger numbers come from better communication or simply from serving wealthier clients. A veterinary performance system needs to bring these metrics together into one view and update them often enough that a practice manager notices changes within weeks instead of discovering them in a year-end report, when the clients or staff involved may already be gone.

The practical takeaway is not to measure everything at once because that usually creates a dashboard that nobody actually uses. Instead, choose one metric from each category—active clients, new client acquisition, gross revenue per square foot, staff turnover, and average client transaction—and review them every week or every month instead of only occasionally. The AVMA's own advice to practice owners at its 2025 forum was to make better use of the reporting features already available in their practice management software instead of assuming better performance measurement requires entirely new tools. Most veterinary clinics already have the data they need inside their PIMS. What is usually missing is a consistent process for bringing those five or six key metrics into one place and reviewing them before, not after, a slow quarter makes the problem obvious.
